title: Dirty Dancing: Havana Nights
full_review:
An American teenager is transformed from a fox-trotting bookworm to a hot-tamale samba sensation in just a few easy dance lessons in "Dirty Dancing: Havana Nights" (Artisan).

More a re-imagining than a remake, director Guy Ferland's film hits all the narrative beats of the "inspired-by" original, "Dirty Dancing" (1987). But despite its setting being spiced up from a Borscht-belt Catskills resort in 1963 to the political hothouse of a Havana luxury hotel on the eve of the Cuban revolution, the movie lacks the flavor of the original. Like its predecessor, it does, however, still have plenty of sweaty, gyrating bodies -- and Patrick Swayze (in a small role as a dance instructor).

Romola Garai stars as Katey Miller, a Pollyanna dragged to Cuba by her father's new job for Chrysler. Katey is brainy, a point driven home by repeated references to her attending Radcliffe come the fall. She is also repressed -- conveyed via cliche by her wearing a wool cardigan sweater around the hotel's pool while her silver-spoon peers sunbathe in bikinis.

But her Ivy League ambitions and puritanical prissiness evaporate like the smoke from a Cuban cigar as soon as she meets Javier (Diego Luna), a busboy with bedroom eyes and all the right moves. As sole provider for his family, Diego quietly suffers the daily indignities of carting drinks and towels to the spoiled scions of the very American fat cats his Fidelista brother (Rene Lavan) is trying to oust from the country.

But when a spilled drink and a chivalrous walk home get Javier fired, Katey, feeling responsible, signs them up for a New Year's Eve dance contest with a grand prize of $5,000. Of course, when planning such an event, one should always double-check to make sure there are no Marxist revolutions scheduled for the same night.

John Slattery and Sela Ward play Katey's parents, themselves no strangers to cutting the rug, and, as in the original, also voice objections to their daughter fraternizing -- let alone dirty dancing -- with the hired help.

Despite a picturesque surf-and-sunset backdrop (with Puerto Rico convincingly passing for Batista-era Cuba), Ferland saddles the clash-of-cultures love affair with a political subplot. But rather than add depth to the characters and story, the glossy, faux weightiness only magnifies the superficiality of the script.
Katey's parents (the film's most visible authority figures) are generally cast in a sympathetic light, but the eroticism of the movie's choppily edited, bump-and-grind choreography imparts a misleading message that seems to equate personal fulfillment with sensual liberation.

It shouldn't be hard to find something better to do with your Havana nights.

Due to an implied sexual encounter and brief violence, as well as some mild crass expressions and a racial slur, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
